newsitem.title: SPAIN: Spain's Rojo eyes strict budget, lower inflation.
newsitem.headline: Spain's Rojo eyes strict budget, lower inflation.

text.p: The Bank of Spain has been sparing in sanctioning interest rate declines but a strict 1997 budget would increase its room to manoeuvre, Governor Luis Angel Rojo told a parliamentary committee on Wednesday.
"This difficulty (of fighting inflation) explains the Bank of Spain's prudence in administering the scope available to reduce its interest rates," Rojo told an economic commission.
The Bank of Spain has reduced its key money market rate five times this year, cutting it to 7.25 percent now from nine percent at the beginning of January.
But it has held off since early June, and many economists link its reluctance to the upcoming budget.
They believe the central bank wants assurance the government will deliver to parliament this month as austere a budget as it has promised.

The conservatives have pledged that their draft would slash the deficit to three percent of gross domestic product from a projected 4.4 percent this year - one of the conditions set out in the Maastricht Treaty for joining in the launch of Europe's single currency.

"Approval of a budget which responds to expectations (of reaching the Maastricht criteria for the public deficit)...will increase the margin for monetary policy to more easily reach the forecast for inflation targets," Rojo said.

Spanish bonds moved higher after Rojo's comments, which were intrepreted as a sign that the central bank was likely to cut its key money market interest rate by 25 basis points at the first repo auction after the budget, on October 3.

"At the end of the day, even if they don't reach the Maastricht criteria the budget is still going to be fiscally restrictive, which is positive," said Mark Geddes, senior economist at independent London research company 4Cast Ltd.
"The real economy is still weak and fiscal toughness has to be offset. With mark/peseta at current levels, there's still plenty of scope to cut rates," he said.
The central bank governor's inflation concerns were mainly focused on moderate wage growth.
"The acceleration of unit wage costs ....is the greatest obstacle for the necessary reduction in the overall inflation rate to materialise," Rojo said.
But despite the difficulties, Rojo was relatively upbeat on the outlook.
"Current conditions of the Spanish economy are favourable to taking on the effort of reducing inflation," he said.
The Bank of Spain expects a CPI of under 3.5 percent by the end of the year, moving below 3.0 percent next year.

But a recent pick-up in consumer price inflation, which was at 3.7 percent year-on-year in both July and August, was "transitory, as it was based on the most volatile components of the index," he said.
